task_row_model.query: What strategic and logistical factors caused Napoleon's 1812 invasion of Russia to fail?

documents.content: Academic analysis of Grand Armée logistics during the 1812 campaign emphasizes scale and infrastructure limits. Napoleon assembled roughly 610,000 men drawn from across Europe, creating a force that required vast quantities of food, fodder and ammunition. As the army advanced, supply lines lengthened over poor roads and rivers, relying on horse-drawn wagons and depots increasingly distant from the front. Contemporary staff reports cite frequent wagon shortages and delays; without local requisitioned stores the advancing columns often outpaced their supplies. Russian retreat tactics deliberately denied resources to the invaders, implementing a scorched-earth policy that left little forage or grain for foraging parties.
documents.reasoning_trace: Extracted initial Grand Armée size (≈610,000), overstretched supply lines over poor roads, dependence on wagon trains and depots, and Russian scorched-earth denial of local supplies.

documents.content: Newspaper-style account of the occupation of Moscow and the campaign's turn toward disaster: Napoleon occupied Moscow in September, but municipal authorities and the civilian population had largely abandoned the city and fires destroyed substantial stores. With no viable supply stockpiles to requisition and winter approaching, the French commander found his army exposed. Eyewitnesses reported unusually early and severe winter weather that year; column diaries record plummeting temperatures and widespread exposure. Lack of shelter compounded malnutrition and disease. After waiting in Moscow for weeks without resupply, the army began a retrograde movement, during which cold, hunger and sickness produced heavy casualties.
documents.reasoning_trace: Notes occupation of Moscow which was abandoned and burned, absence of supplies in the city, onset of severe winter, exposure, disease and starvation forcing a retreat.

documents.content: Informal regimental memorandum and campaign notes detail the day-to-day collapse of operational capability. Party dispatches mention frequent partisan and Cossack attacks on the long supply convoys, leading to loss of wagons, horses and rations. Cavalry strength diminished from losses of mounts, reducing reconnaissance and escort capacity. With supply columns harried and local forage scarce due to earlier Russian removal, units began cannibalizing supplies and suffered desertion. Attrition figures in rear-area reports are stark: from the massive initial entry only a fraction remained by late autumn and into December—reports estimate survivors numbering in the low tens of thousands.
documents.reasoning_trace: Identifies partisan attacks on supply convoys, loss of wagons and horses, reduced cavalry and escort capability, resulting desertion and attrition to low tens of thousands by December.

documents.content: Reference entry on Napoleonic strategy offers contextual but general material: Napoleon's doctrine favored decisive battle and rapid campaigning, with administrative departments organizing provisioning through standardized requisition forms and regional supply depots. Earlier campaigns in Central Europe encountered different logistics challenges because of denser road networks and friendlier hinterlands. Entries include terminology—'Grande Armée' as the umbrella force, supply 'système de ravitaillement'—and retellings of diplomatic objectives, but they do not provide operational specifics for the Russian theater. Several paragraphs reiterate the organizational model and past reforms in commissariat procedures.

task_row_model.golden_answer: Napoleon’s invasion failed because a very large Grand Armée (~610,000) outpaced its logistical base: long wagon-dependent supply lines over poor roads were repeatedly disrupted by partisan attacks, and Russian scorched-earth tactics left no local forage. Occupied Moscow offered no supplies after fires, severe winter and exposure set in, and disease, starvation and attrition reduced the force to only low tens of thousands by December.
